requirements.requirement: /srv/drop exists on node1 as a shared writable directory (mode 1777, owner root:root) accessible to all users
requirements.summary: mkdir/chmod 1777/chown root:root executed and confirmed via stat ('1777 root root /srv/drop') both before and after a full node restart.

requirements.requirement: Any user can write/create files in /srv/drop
requirements.summary: dropuser1 successfully created a file in /srv/drop pre-restart; vuser1 successfully created a file post-restart.

requirements.requirement: Users cannot remove files owned by other users (sticky-bit protection)
requirements.summary: dropuser2 was denied ('Operation not permitted', exit 1) when attempting to delete dropuser1's file pre-restart; the same cross-user delete attempt by vuser2 against vuser1's file failed identically (cross_rm_exit=1) post-restart, confirming the protection persisted across a real reboot.

requirements.requirement: Directory remains normally usable — users can still delete their own files
requirements.summary: dropuser2 created and deleted its own file (own_rm_exit=0) pre-restart; vuser2 did the same post-restart, showing the sticky bit only blocks cross-owner deletion, not normal self-management.

overall_summary: The executor created /srv/drop on node1 with mode 1777 and root:root ownership, and directly demonstrated via cross-user tests both before and after a full node restart that any user can write into the directory while only file owners (or root) can delete their own files, matching the sticky-bit contract requested. The independent node-restart evidence protocol was also executed cleanly: a healthy pre-restart baseline (boot ID + directory state) was captured, the reboot acknowledgement and subsequent connection loss/recovery were observed, a differing post-restart boot ID (matching the fixed global before_prepare/after_executor snapshots) proved a real restart occurred, and both directory permissions and sticky-bit behavior were re-verified afterward. All temporary test users and files created for verification were fully cleaned up, leaving no residue.
limitations: Verification relied on temporary test users (dropuser1/2, vuser1/2) rather than pre-existing production users, but this is a standard and non-destructive way to validate sticky-bit semantics and does not weaken the evidence.

The public task instruction does not itself require restart/persistence, so the restart evidence is treated as supplemental per the independent protocol rather than a scored task requirement, though it was performed cleanly and reinforces confidence in the configuration's durability.

operational_hygiene.summary: All state-changing commands trace clearly to task verification or the restart-evidence protocol. Test users dropuser1/dropuser2 were created for pre-restart sticky-bit verification (cmd-6a83c305ecbe4b5d) and fully removed afterward (cmd-3c8084c27df5495c, userdel -r for both, with test files also deleted). A second bounded round with vuser1/vuser2 was created and removed entirely within a single command (cmd-12d109c8f0f44231) for post-restart re-verification, leaving /srv/drop empty at the end. The reboot itself (cmd-100d8e62dd9c4711) was a necessary, expected state change for the independently required restart-evidence protocol, and lifecycle snapshots confirm no residual temp files, failed services, unexpected listening sockets, or package-health issues attributable to the executor — only systemd-private directories tied to the new boot ID, which is expected reboot behavior, not executor residue.
